tier_reason: First-party vendor numbers (VirusTotal blog 'YARA-X just got faster', 2026-05-13, and the docs page yara_vs_yara-x.md) against legacy YARA, with no hardware, compiler, flags, YARA version or build options and a private 500-file corpus; no public harness that runs both scanners. Vendor-blog evidence from the product's owner is tier C.

corrections.why_faster: Not language-level and not the same algorithm. Blog (about the 2.2x gain over the previous YARA-X build, not directly versus YARA): PR #654 swapped the aho_corasick crate for daachorse, a double-array Aho-Corasick with a tighter inner loop and cache-efficient storage that, per the blog, 'mirrors the core design principles of the original C-based YARA engine'; PR #657 groups many 'matches' regexes on one target into one regex RegexSet pass (Livehunt figures compare YARA-X before and after, not YARA). The docs give no mechanism for the bitcoin-regex and loop-rule gaps beyond 'performs better ... with regular expressions and complex hex patterns'; YARA-X ships its own regex engine ('fast-regexp' feature) and evaluates conditions through wasmtime-compiled WebAssembly (Cargo.toml dependency) where YARA interprets its own bytecode, which is a plausible but unstated cause of the loop-rule gap.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated on the blog or docs page. Defaults (not confirmed as what was benchmarked): YARA's Makefile.am adds -O3 when optimization is enabled (the configure default); YARA-X's Cargo.toml has no custom [profile.release], so cargo --release uses opt-level 3 (an optional release-lto profile adds LTO and codegen-units=1).
corrections.caveats: First-party claim from the vendor (VirusTotal, Google) with no hardware, compiler flags, YARA version or build options, and the 500-file corpus is private, so the 1.85x figure is not reproducible by others; tier C. The same blog table shows YARA-X was slower than YARA (57.584 s vs 48.275 s, about 1.19x slower, derived from page data) before the daachorse change in v1.16.0, and the docs concede some rules and files where YARA still wins. The single-rule claims (more than 20 s vs under 1 s for a bitcoin_address regex on a ~200 MB file; 5-6x for a for-loop rule) give no machine, file or version details and target rules YARA itself warns 'may slow down scanning'. The VirusTotal Livehunt figures (p99 over 6 s to under 3 s) compare YARA-X before and after PR #657, not YARA. The win is architectural (different matcher, regex engine and condition execution via wasmtime), not a Rust codegen effect, and both builds' optimisation levels are unstated (defaults are -O3 for YARA and opt-level 3 for YARA-X). Read from the markdown sources inside the repo (site/content/blog/yara-x-just-got-faster/index.md, site/content/docs/intro/yara_vs_yara-x.md); the rendered virustotal.github.io pages are blocked here.

notes: Blog table matches the record exactly (26.152 s daachorse, 57.584 s aho_corasick, 48.275 s legacy YARA, 1.85x stated) and docs claims match verbatim; license BSD-3-Clause, 1.3k stars, last commit 2026-10-09 confirmed. Shortcomings: vendor-only numbers, private corpus, no hardware or build details, YARA-X slower than YARA before v1.16.0, some rules still faster in YARA, win is architectural rather than language-level.

tier_reason: Snippet only: codeberg.org (proxy CONNECT 403), zff.dev (ENOTFOUND) and no GitHub mirror (github.com/imal/grep-zg 404), so the README was never opened; three separate search summaries repeat the 32.7 ms / 38.4 ms / 314 ms row, so first-party numbers exist but their workload and method are unverified. Snippet-only numbers are capped at C; the orchestrator may prefer D because the corpus attribution conflicts.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Snippet only, from search-result summaries of the README (never opened): a 'norm' (normal search) row with zrep 32.7 ms, ripgrep 38.4 ms, GNU grep 314 ms, about 9.6x faster than GNU grep (derived from snippet data); one summary also reports a second table on a 271 MB, 2.5M-line log (warm cache, output piped through cat) with zrep 76 ms, ripgrep 198 ms and GNU grep 248 ms in normal mode (about 3.3x, derived from snippet data), and about 10 ms vs 49 ms (ripgrep) and 52 ms (GNU grep) for a count mode.
corrections.workload: Unverified, snippet summaries conflict: the search agent's snippet described a recursive search for 'stdio.h' under /usr/include (409 MB, 41K files, warm cache, 28 cores, output piped through cat); two later snippets attribute the same 32.7/38.4/314 ms row to a single 205 MB log with 706K matches of 'debug' on 28 cores, and a second table to a 271 MB, 2.5M-line log with output piped through cat to avoid GNU grep's /dev/null shortcut.
corrections.why_faster: Not stated in anything readable here. A search summary describes zrep as a multithreaded grep replacement whose README shows a -j28 usage example, so the 9.6x gap over single-threaded GNU grep is most likely parallelism on 28 cores rather than Zig codegen; ripgrep, also parallel, is within 17 percent in the same row.
corrections.caveats: Snippet only: codeberg.org (proxy CONNECT 403), zff.dev (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND) and the besthub.dev article (ENOTFOUND, and it covers a different 'zg', a semantic search tool) were unreachable, and there is no GitHub mirror, so the README, license, code, build mode and benchmark method were never opened; every figure and the language (Zig, Zig 0.15.2 per the earlier snippet) come from search-result summaries. The summaries disagree on which corpus the 32.7/38.4/314 ms row measured (/usr/include recursive vs a 205 MB log), and one says that row wrote to /dev/null while a second table piped output through cat. One machine, warm cache, a multi-threaded tool against single-threaded GNU grep, so the ratio is mostly parallelism; GNU grep's build (distro -O2 or otherwise) and zrep's Zig release mode are unknown. License, stars and last commit unverified. Low confidence; re-open the Codeberg README when a session can reach it and drop to D if the numbers differ.

notes: Could not open any primary source (Codeberg blocked, zff.dev unresolvable, no GitHub mirror); kept at C on consistent snippet numbers but corpus attribution conflicts between snippets and the gap is likely threads, not Zig. Shortcomings: snippet only, unverified workload, multi-threaded vs single-threaded GNU grep, license and maintenance unknown, low notability.

tier_reason: Upgraded from D: the 2026-02-22 PNG charts on the performance page plot wall-clock times for mlr-5.10.3 (C) against mlr-6.0.0 to 6.17.0 (Go) on an Apple M1 MacBook Air, from the public script scripts/perf/time-verbs.py; first-party, numbers only readable from charts, and the Go version and the Miller 5 build flags for these runs are unstated, so not A.

corrections.baseline: Miller 5.10.3, the earlier C implementation of the same tool (charts label it mlr-5.10.3); the docs explicitly decline to compare with awk, sort or cut
corrections.claimed_speedup: Read from the 2026-02-22 charts on docs/src/performance.md (approximate, y-axis is seconds per scripts/perf/time-verbs.py, mlr-5.10.3 vs mlr-6.17.0, one-million-record files, Apple M1): then-chains of put chain-1 about 3.8 s vs 1.6 s and chain-4 about 10.2 s vs 2.15 s (about 2.4x and 4.7x, derived from chart reading); CSV verbs stats1 about 1.8 s vs 0.9 s (about 2x), sort-n about 2.9 s vs 2.5 s, sort-f about 1.7 s vs 1.4 s, tac about 1.6 s vs 1.3 s, check and tail about 0.85-0.9 s vs 0.8 s; format cats cat-csv about 1.5 s vs 0.8 s, cat-xtab about 3.15 s vs 1.1 s, cat-dkvp about 1.5 s vs 1.2 s, cat-csvlite about equal, but Miller 6 is slower on cat-nidx (about 0.9 s vs 3.2 s) and cat-json (about 6.3 s vs 8.7 s). Page text: 'CSV processing was particularly improved in Miller 6'; 'Even single-verb processing with put and stats1 was significantly faster on both platforms'; JSON 'Miller 5 did better than Miller 6 but only on Linux, not Mac'.
corrections.hardware: MacBook Air with Apple M1 (early 2026 runs, charts dated 2026-02-22); the Linux machine mentioned in the notes is not described
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the 2026 runs: the Go 1.15.15, 1.16.12, 1.17.5 and 1.18beta1 list is from late-2021 benchmarking; how the mlr-5.10.3 binary was built is not stated (the Miller 5.10.3 autotools build uses AM_CFLAGS -Wall -std=gnu99 plus autoconf's default -g -O2 per the c/Makefile.am link-line comment, not -O3)
corrections.workload: scripts/perf/time-verbs.py: average wall-clock time of 5 runs per case (process spawned via the shell, output to /dev/null) for mlr check, cat, tail, tac, sort -f, sort -n, stats1 and put then-chains of depth 1-4 on a one-million-record CSV made by scripts/perf/prep-perf-data.sh (example.csv repeated 100000 times, shuffled, with added fields), plus mlr cat over its CSV, CSV-lite, DKVP, NIDX, XTAB and JSON conversions.
corrections.why_faster: Not the language's codegen: docs/src/cpu.md says Miller 6 runs two reader goroutines, one goroutine per verb in a then-chain and a writer goroutine connected by channels (typically 250-350 percent CPU on deep chains), while Miller 5 is single-threaded, which explains the then-chain gap growing with chain depth; the CSV reader and writer were rewritten in the Go version, and the page gives no mechanism for the single-verb gains. Different architecture, so same_algorithm stays false.
corrections.caveats: First-party, numbers only in PNG charts (values read approximately), one M1 laptop, average of 5 runs including process startup. Miller 6 is not uniformly faster: in the same 2026-02-22 run it is about 3.5x slower on NIDX cat and about 1.4x slower on JSON cat than Miller 5.10.3, and the page says Miller 5 beat Miller 6 on JSON on Linux. The large then-chain wins come from Miller 6 spreading reader, verbs and writer over several cores against single-threaded C Miller 5, not from Go codegen. Miller 5's build for these runs is unstated and its default autotools build is -g -O2, not the -O3 wave 14 asks for. The 'Before/After' June 2026 tables and the 2026-06-20 charts compare Miller 6.18.1 with 6.19.0 only; their faster numbers (for example chain-4 about 0.96 s) come from a separate run and must not be compared with the Miller 5 points (cross-run). The same page times system cut (C) at 1m8.3s real against mlr cut at 1m27.6s real (3m8.9s user) on a 40-million-record CSV, so Miller 6 is slower than cut there, though the docs say such comparisons are not apples-to-apples. Miller 5 is a same-tool predecessor, not the C incumbent (awk, cut, sort) most developers use.

notes: Record said the charts were unreadable; I read the 2026-02-22 PNGs and they hold Miller 5.10.3 vs 6.x times, so the tier rises D to C (verdict confirm with upgrade). Shortcomings: chart-only first-party numbers, Miller 6 slower on NIDX and JSON, chain wins are multicore vs single-threaded, Miller 5 build unstated (default -O2), slower than system cut on the page's cell_towers example. License BSD-2-Clause, 10.0k stars, last commit 2026-09-29 confirmed.
